missing_spec_content.spec_text: Some atomic nuclei are unstable. The nucleus gives out radiation as it changes to become more stable.
missing_spec_content.why: The lesson says decay is spontaneous and random (introTips[0]). It never says that the nuclei are unstable, or that emitting radiation makes the nucleus more stable.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: Activity is the rate at which a source of unstable nuclei decays. Activity is measured in becquerel (Bq)
missing_spec_content.why: Activity and its unit, the becquerel, are not taught anywhere. Becquerel appears only as a person's name in the intro.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: Count-rate is the number of decays recorded each second by a detector (eg Geiger-Muller tube).
missing_spec_content.why: Count-rate and detectors such as the Geiger-Muller tube are not mentioned.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: The nuclear radiation emitted may be: ... a neutron (n).
missing_spec_content.why: The lesson presents only three types of radiation ("It turned out to be three completely different types of radiation"). Neutron emission is omitted.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: Students should be able to apply their knowledge to the uses of radiation and evaluate the best sources of radiation to use in a given situation.
missing_spec_content.why: Uses are only listed in the intro ("cancer treatments, smoke detectors, carbon dating"). There is no teaching on choosing the best source for a given use based on penetration, range and ionising power.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: man-made sources such as the fallout from nuclear weapons testing and nuclear accidents.
missing_spec_content.why: keyPoints[3].content lists medical uses, power stations and weapons testing, but not nuclear accidents. It also does not use the word "fallout".

missing_spec_content.spec_text: The level of background radiation and radiation dose may be affected by occupation and/or location.
missing_spec_content.why: The lesson does not teach that background level and dose vary with occupation or location.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: Radiation dose is measured in sieverts (Sv) 1000 millisieverts (mSv) = 1 sievert (Sv)
missing_spec_content.why: Radiation dose, sieverts and the mSv to Sv conversion are not covered. Recall of the unit is not required, but students must be able to use it.

above_gcse.text: Note: a neutrino is also given out, but you don't need to include it at GCSE.
above_gcse.why: Neutrinos are not in the specification and could confuse the student when writing beta decay equations.
This puts the neutrino into a bullet the student is meant to write down, even though the specification does not include it.
The specification states "The identification of daughter elements from such decays is not required."

above_gcse.text: Natural sources (~85% in the UK): ... Artificial sources (~15%)
above_gcse.why: The specification requires only the types of source, not percentage contributions or specific isotopes such as potassium-40.

above_gcse.text: The nucleus is still in an excited state. It releases its extra energy as a gamma ray.
above_gcse.why: Excited nuclear states go beyond the specification, which says only "electromagnetic radiation from the nucleus".

factual_errors.correction: Gamma rays have a long range in air, from many metres up to kilometres. Their intensity falls with distance and they are gradually absorbed, so the range is not infinite. A better entry is 'very long (many metres or more)'.

factual_errors.text: Background radiation is always present and comes from natural sources.
factual_errors.correction: Background radiation comes from natural sources and from man-made sources, such as fallout from nuclear weapons testing and nuclear accidents. This tip also contradicts keyPoints[3].content.

wrong_terms.spec_term: atomic number / mass number (the spec does not use the symbols Z and A)

not_checked: The specification text is missing the symbols for the alpha particle and beta particle, and both example nuclear equations in 4.4.2.2. I could not check the lesson's notation (⁴₂He, ⁰₋₁e) or its examples against the exact spec symbols. I checked them against my own knowledge only, and they are consistent.
Whether the superscript and subscript characters in the nuclear equations display correctly to the student was not checked.
